title: Nervous and Endocrine Systems
seo_title: Grade 6 Science: Nervous and Endocrine Systems Worksheets (BC Curriculum)
standard_text: Multicellular organisms rely on internal systems to survive, reproduce and interact with their environment: the basic structures and functions of the nervous and hormonal (endocrine) systems. (summary of BC's Curriculum, Science 6, Biology)
meta_desc: Free Grade 6 science worksheets (BC): the brain, spinal cord and nerves, receptors and responses, reflexes, and hormones. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Nerves send fast signals; hormones send slow ones.
key_sub: The brain and spinal cord control the body.
body_html:
How to think about it

The nervous system is the brain, spinal cord and nerves. Receptors in the sense organs detect a stimulus, nerves carry the signal to the brain or spinal cord, and a response is sent to muscles or glands. A reflex is a fast, automatic response that goes through the spinal cord.

The endocrine (hormonal) system uses glands that release hormones into the blood. Hormones act more slowly but last longer: insulin controls blood sugar, adrenaline prepares the body for action, and growth hormone controls growth.

Example

You touch a hot pan and pull away before you feel pain. What is this?

The signal goes through the spinal cord.

Answer: a reflex

Example

How do hormones travel around the body?

They are released by glands.

Answer: in the blood

Common mistakes

  • Thinking every response goes through the brain first.
  • Mixing up nerves (fast) and hormones (slow).
  • Thinking the sense organ makes the decision.

faq.q: What is the job of the spinal cord?
faq.a: It carries messages between the brain and the body and handles reflexes.

items.q: Noah notices a wet, slippery floor and walks slowly. Which shows the path of the message in order?
c: receptors → sensory nerves → brain → motor nerves → muscles
muscles → motor nerves → brain → sensory nerves → receptors
items.e: Stimulus → receptor → sensory neuron → brain → motor neuron → muscle (response).

items.q: Lucas is learning about receptors. Which receptors respond to the pitch of a song?
items.e: Receptors in the ears respond to the pitch of a song and send messages to the brain.

items.q: Liam notices the smell of smoke and leaves the building. Which part of the body decides how to respond?
items.e: Receptors detect; the brain processes and decides; muscles carry out the response.

items.q: Owen is learning about receptors. Which receptors respond to chemicals in food?
items.e: Taste buds on the tongue respond to chemicals in food and send messages to the brain.

items.q: Which system sends fast electrical messages along neurons?
items.e: Nerve impulses take milliseconds.

items.q: Which hormone lowers blood glucose?
items.e: Insulin is made by the pancreas.

items.q: Amira measures reaction times by catching a dropped ruler: 18, 15, 13 and 12 cm on four tries. What pattern does she see?
c: Her reaction time improves with practice.
items.e: A shorter catch distance means a faster reaction.

items.q: Liam measures pulse rate before and after exercise. Why should he take readings until it is steady again?
c: to see how long negative feedback takes to return it to normal
items.e: Recovery time shows fitness.

items.q: A doctor taps below a patient's knee and the leg kicks. What is this?
items.e: The knee-jerk reflex goes through the spinal cord.

items.q: Ava tests reaction time with sound (a clap) and with sight (a light). How can she make it a fair test?
c: use the same people, the same number of trials and change only the type of stimulus
items.e: Only one variable should change.

items.q: Hana drinks 1 L of water and collects her urine each hour. What pattern would she expect?
c: more urine for a few hours, then back to normal
items.e: The kidneys remove extra water by negative feedback.

items.q: Jayden tests whether music affects reaction time. Which variable should he keep the same?
c: the person, the ruler and the drop height
items.e: Only the music should change.

items.q: What is homeostasis?
c: keeping conditions inside the body, such as temperature, steady
items.e: Body temperature stays near 37 °C.

items.q: Jayden's average ruler drop was 20 cm with his writing hand and 25 cm with his other hand. What can he conclude?
c: The ruler was heavier the second time.
He reacts faster with his writing hand.
He reacts faster with his other hand.
items.e: Shorter distance means faster reaction.

items.q: What happens to blood vessels near the skin when you are too hot?
c: They narrow to keep heat in.
They widen so more heat is lost (vasodilation).
items.e: Red, flushed skin shows this.

items.q: Which system sends chemical messages (hormones) in the blood?
items.e: Hormones are slower but last longer.

items.q: Emma covers one eye and tries to touch two pencil tips together. It is harder. Why?
c: Hands need both eyes to move.
The brain uses information from both eyes to judge distance.
items.e: The brain combines information from receptors.

items.q: Mei records a runner's body temperature: 37.0 °C, 38.2 °C after the race, 37.1 °C after 20 minutes rest. What does this show?
c: Negative feedback returned the temperature to normal.
items.e: Sweating and vasodilation cooled the runner.

items.q: A surf lifesaver on Bondi Beach has hot, red skin on a summer day. Which two responses are cooling him?
c: sweating and widening of skin blood vessels
items.e: Both release heat from the body.

items.q: Noah tests his reaction time with his right hand (writing hand) and left hand: 0.21 s and 0.27 s. What could he conclude?
c: His writing hand reacts faster, perhaps because of practice.
items.e: Repeat with more people to check.

items.q: Why does a person who has been stung by a bee jump away from a buzzing sound later?
c: The brain stored a memory of the sting and uses it to respond.
It is a new reflex every time.
items.e: Memory guides behaviour.

items.q: In type 1 diabetes, what does the pancreas fail to make?
items.e: People with type 1 diabetes inject insulin or use a pump.

items.q: What is a stimulus?
c: a change in the environment that the body detects
items.e: A hot stove or a loud noise is a stimulus.

items.q: What does negative feedback do?
c: only happens when you are sick
reverses a change to bring a condition back to normal
items.e: Negative does not mean bad.

items.q: How do plants reduce water loss in drought?
c: abscisic acid causes the stomata to close
items.e: Abscisic acid is a stress hormone.

items.q: Leah's blood glucose is 8.5 mmol/L (normal is about 4–7 mmol/L). Which hormone does the pancreas release more of?
items.e: High glucose → insulin; low glucose → glucagon.

items.q: Compare nervous and hormonal control. For nervous control, what is the area affected?
items.e: Nervous: fast, electrical, short-lived, precise. Hormonal: slower, chemical in blood, longer-lasting, widespread.

items.q: Arjun's blood glucose is 3.0 mmol/L (normal is about 4–7 mmol/L). Which hormone does the pancreas release more of?
items.e: High glucose → insulin; low glucose → glucagon.

c: Glycogen is converted to glucose, which is released into the blood.
Glucose is converted to glycogen and stored.
items.e: Insulin and glucagon both act on the liver.

they have a larger surface area to volume ratio

items.q: Ethan is studying the bones. Which organ system is this body part in?
items.e: The bones is part of the skeletal system, which supports the body and protects organs.

items.q: Ava asks: what is the main job of the nervous system?
c: It collects information and sends messages that control the body.
It supports the body and protects organs.
It removes wastes from the body.
It moves blood that carries oxygen and nutrients to every cell.
items.e: The nervous system collects information and sends messages that control the body.

items.q: Mateo asks: what is the main job of the digestive system?
c: It takes in oxygen and gets rid of carbon dioxide.
It removes wastes from the body.
It supports the body and protects organs.
It breaks food down into nutrients the body can use.
items.e: The digestive system breaks food down into nutrients the body can use.

items.q: Chloe is studying the blood vessels. Which organ system is this body part in?
items.e: The blood vessels is part of the circulatory system, which moves blood that carries oxygen and nutrients to every cell.

items.q: Arjun writes in a health journal: “You touch a hot pan and pull your hand back.” Which two body systems work together most here?
items.e: Nerves send a message to the brain, and muscles move the hand.

items.q: Kai is studying the brain. Which organ system is this body part in?
items.e: The brain is part of the nervous system, which collects information and sends messages that control the body.

items.q: Kai reads about a body system that breaks food down into nutrients the body can use. Which system is it?
items.e: The digestive system breaks food down into nutrients the body can use.

items.q: Zoe is studying the skull. Which organ system is this body part in?
items.e: The skull is part of the skeletal system, which supports the body and protects organs.

items.q: Ethan reads about a body system that takes in oxygen and gets rid of carbon dioxide. Which system is it?
items.e: The respiratory system takes in oxygen and gets rid of carbon dioxide.

items.q: Ethan reads about a body system that collects information and sends messages that control the body. Which system is it?
items.e: The nervous system collects information and sends messages that control the body.

items.q: Noah writes in a health journal: “You run a race and breathe hard.” Which two body systems work together most here?
items.e: The lungs take in more oxygen, and the heart pumps faster to carry it to the muscles.

items.q: Nathan is studying the small intestine. Which organ system is this body part in?
items.e: The small intestine is part of the digestive system, which breaks food down into nutrients the body can use.

items.q: Owen writes in a health journal: “You exercise and start to sweat.” Which two body systems work together most here?
items.e: Blood carries heat to the skin, and sweat helps cool you.

items.q: Noah writes in a health journal: “You catch a ball thrown to you.” Which two body systems work together most here?
items.e: The eyes and brain track the ball, and muscles move your hands.

items.q: Emma writes in a health journal: “You climb stairs quickly.” Which two body systems work together most here?
items.e: Leg muscles work hard and need more oxygen from the lungs.

items.q: Lucas is studying the trachea (windpipe). Which organ system is this body part in?
items.e: The trachea (windpipe) is part of the respiratory system, which takes in oxygen and gets rid of carbon dioxide.

items.q: Mateo asks: what is the main job of the excretory system?
c: It breaks food down into nutrients the body can use.
It collects information and sends messages that control the body.
It removes wastes from the body.
It moves the body by pulling on bones.
items.e: The excretory system removes wastes from the body.

items.q: Leah is studying the tendons. Which organ system is this body part in?
items.e: The tendons is part of the muscular system, which moves the body by pulling on bones.

items.q: Ethan asks: what is the main job of the respiratory system?
c: It breaks food down into nutrients the body can use.
It removes wastes from the body.
It supports the body and protects organs.
It takes in oxygen and gets rid of carbon dioxide.
items.e: The respiratory system takes in oxygen and gets rid of carbon dioxide.

items.q: Kai is studying the blood. Which organ system is this body part in?
items.e: The blood is part of the circulatory system, which moves blood that carries oxygen and nutrients to every cell.
